**The Last Letter**

I found it in the attic, folded neatly between the dusty shelves of my grandfather’s books. The paper was yellowed with age, the edges slightly frayed, as if it had been tucked away for decades. I unfolded it carefully, my fingers trembling slightly, and there it was—his handwriting, slow and deliberate, as if he were writing to someone he’d never meet.

*Dear [Name],*

*I don’t know if you’ll ever read this. I don’t know if you’ll ever know me. But I have to write it. I have to say it.*

*You see, I was never the kind of man who kept secrets. Not from my family, not from my friends. But this… this is something I can’t unsee. Something I can’t undo.*

*It happened in the summer of 1967. I was working at the old mill, the one that’s been standing for a hundred years. The workers were striking, the air thick with tension. One night, after the others had gone home, I stayed behind to check the machinery. The lights were flickering, the hum of the engines a low, ominous growl. And then—*

*I saw it. A figure in the shadows, too tall, too still. It wasn’t a man. It wasn’t a woman. It was something else. Something that shouldn’t have been there.*

*I ran. I told the foreman, but he laughed it off. Said it was just the wind. Said I was drunk. But I wasn’t drunk. I was terrified. And now, years later, I’m afraid. Afraid that whatever was out there that night is still out there. Afraid that it’s watching me. Afraid that it’s watching you.*

*I don’t know what to do. I don’t know if I can ever go back to the mill. I don’t know if I can ever look at the old factory the same way again. But I have to tell you this. Because if you ever find this letter, if you ever hear whispers of the mill at night…*

*Run.*

*Yours in silence,*
*[Grandfather’s Name]*

I set the letter down, my breath shallow. The attic was cold, the air stale with the scent of old paper and forgotten things. I didn’t know what to think. Was it a warning? A confession? Or just the ramblings of a man who had spent too many nights alone?

I decided to keep it. Not out of fear, but because I wanted to know the truth. Because sometimes, the things we don’t understand are the ones that haunt us the most.

And so, I tucked it back into the attic, where it would stay—until the day I had to read it again.
